CausalChain: Overexpression of MALAT1 in cancer cells -> Formation of a stable triple helix structure -> Scaffold function for recruitment of glycolytic enzymes -> Enhanced local glycolytic activity and metabolic reprogramming -> Promotion of tumor growth; therefore, disruption of the triple helix with small molecules -> Inhibition of enzyme recruitment -> Reversal of metabolic reprogramming -> Reduced tumor progression
Hypothesis: The conserved triple helix structure of MALAT1 acts as a scaffold for glycolytic enzymes in cancer cells, thereby enhancing glycolysis and facilitating tumor metabolic reprogramming. Targeting this structural motif with small molecules will disrupt the lncRNA-enzyme interaction, leading to altered metabolic flux and inhibited tumor growth.
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the multifaceted roles of long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in cell regulation, with emerging evidence suggesting that specific structural motifs are critical for their function. Building on observations of the conserved triple helix structure at the 3′ end of MALAT1, we propose that certain nuclear lncRNAs serve as dynamic scaffolds for key metabolic enzymes. In cancer cells, this interaction may enhance glycolytic flux and promote metabolic reprogramming needed for rapid proliferation. Here, we hypothesize that disrupting the structural integrity of the MALAT1 triple helix using small-molecule compounds will prevent the recruitment of glycolytic enzymes, thereby reversing metabolic shifts that favor tumor growth. This novel perspective uniting lncRNA structure with enzymatic modulation of metabolism opens the door for targeted metabolic interventions in oncology.
